subject: Environment
topic: Green technology and renewable energy II — mixed tiers
description: Solar, wind, green hydrogen, carbon capture, India's RE targets

questions.stem: India's National Solar Mission was launched as part of which broader climate-action plan?

options.option_text: National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC)

questions.explanation: NAPCC (launched 2008) is India's flagship climate-policy umbrella with EIGHT National Missions — Solar (JNNSM), Enhanced Energy Efficiency, Sustainable Habitat, Water, Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem, Green India, Sustainable Agriculture, Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change. JNNSM's revised target (2015) — 100 GW solar by 2022 (not fully met); overall renewable 500 GW by 2030 is the current headline. Green India Mission is a SEPARATE mission within NAPCC.

questions.stem: 'Green hydrogen' differs from 'grey hydrogen' primarily in that it is produced by:

options.option_text: Steam methane reforming of natural gas
Electrolysis of water using renewable electricity

questions.explanation: Hydrogen-colour palette — 'green' H₂ is produced by electrolysis of water powered by renewables (zero CO₂); 'grey' H₂ from steam-methane reforming (most today); 'blue' H₂ is grey + carbon capture; 'brown/black' H₂ is from coal gasification. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission (Jan 2023) targets 5 million tonnes of green H₂ production annually by 2030.

questions.stem: India's first and largest solar park is located in:
questions.explanation: Bhadla Solar Park in Jodhpur district, Rajasthan — capacity ~2,245 MW — was completed in 2020 and is one of the largest solar installations in the world. Rajasthan's high solar irradiance and flat terrain suit it well. Pavagada (Karnataka, ~2,050 MW) and Kurnool (AP, ~1,000 MW) are close runners. India's total installed solar capacity has crossed 80 GW (2024).

questions.stem: Which Indian state leads in installed wind-power capacity?
questions.explanation: Tamil Nadu has historically led — the Muppandal Wind Farm in Kanyakumari is one of the country's largest. Gujarat has overtaken TN in recent years for new capacity additions (Bhavnagar, Kachchh). Top wind states (2024) — Gujarat and Tamil Nadu are near-equal; Karnataka, Maharashtra, Rajasthan follow. India's total wind capacity is ~45 GW. Offshore wind projects off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu coasts are being developed.

questions.stem: The International Solar Alliance (ISA), co-founded by India in 2015, has its headquarters in:
questions.explanation: ISA — launched at the 2015 Paris Climate Summit by PM Modi and French President Hollande — has its HQ at the National Institute of Solar Energy campus in Gurugram, Haryana. It is the first inter-governmental organisation HQ in India. Originally open to 121 sunshine-rich countries between the Tropics; now membership is open to all UN members (124+ signatories).

questions.stem: Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS) technology works by:

options.option_text: Absorbing CO₂ from trees and burying it
Capturing CO₂ from industrial sources and storing it underground
Converting CO₂ directly to oxygen in the atmosphere
Using bacteria to break CO₂ into elements

questions.explanation: CCS traps CO₂ at industrial sources (power plants, cement, steel), compresses it, and injects it into deep geological formations — depleted oil/gas reservoirs, saline aquifers, basalt rock. CCU (Capture and Utilisation) uses it in products like carbonated drinks, concrete. Direct Air Capture (DAC) pulls CO₂ from ambient air — newer, much costlier per tonne. IPCC considers CCS essential for hard-to-abate sectors (steel, cement, heavy industry).

questions.stem: 'Net zero' emissions, a common target in climate policy, means:

options.option_text: Emissions are balanced by equivalent removals

questions.explanation: Net-zero — residual emissions from hard-to-abate activities are matched by CO₂ removals (afforestation, CCS, direct air capture) so the NET balance is zero. Not literally zero emissions. India's target — net zero by 2070 (announced Nov 2021 at COP-26). Global goal to meet Paris 1.5 °C — net zero by ~2050 for major economies. Corporate 'net-zero' pledges often rely heavily on carbon offsets, which are contested.
